claims.text: High-thermal-load processing of AlCrFeNiSi powder creates significant thermal gradients.
Thermal gradients generated during high-thermal-load processing cause residual stresses in AlCrFeNiSi components.
High-thermal-load processing promotes non-equilibrium microstructures that degrade the mechanical performance of AlCrFeNiSi components.
Binder jet printing deposits a liquid binder on powder layers at near-room temperature.
AlCrFeNiSi binder-jetted parts can be consolidated by sintering at 600–800°C in a reducing atmosphere.
Several hours of sintering within 600–800°C can be optimized to achieve complete densification of AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
Binder jet printing followed by low-temperature sintering will produce a more homogeneous, near-equilibrium AlCrFeNiSi microstructure.
Binder jet printing followed by low-temperature sintering will lower dislocation density in AlCrFeNiSi components.
Avoiding localized melting and rapid solidification greatly reduces thermal gradients relative to high-energy additive manufacturing.
Reduced thermal gradients and lower dislocation densities limit residual-stress formation.
Low-temperature sintering densifies AlCrFeNiSi without reintroducing high thermal stresses.
Binder-jetted and sintered components will have significantly lower residual thermal stresses than components produced by conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Binder-jetted and sintered components will have higher ductility than conventionally manufactured high-thermal-load AM components.
Binder-jetted and sintered components will have improved fatigue resilience relative to conventionally manufactured high-thermal-load AM components.
Binder jet processing will reduce overall processing complexity because it requires less thermal management.
Incomplete densification or binder residue may limit the benefits of the proposed route when sintering is not fully optimized.
